title: Chapter 17 — Of Usurpation
paragraphs: Just as conquest may be called a foreign usurpation, so usurpation is a kind of domestic conquest. There is this difference, though: a usurper can never have right on his side, since there is no usurpation except where someone has got possession of what another has a right to. Usurpation, so far as it is only usurpation, is a change of persons alone, not of the forms and rules of the government. For if the usurper extends his power beyond what rightfully belonged to the lawful princes or governors of the commonwealth, that is tyranny added to usurpation.

In all lawful governments, the designation of the persons who are to rule is as natural and necessary a part of the government as its form, and it is something that was originally established by the people. The anarchy is much the same whether there is no form of government at all, or whether people agree that it shall be monarchical but lay down no way of designating the person who is to have the power and be the monarch. That is why all commonwealths, along with their established form of government, also have rules for appointing those who are to have any share in the public authority, and settled methods of conveying the right to them. For the anarchy is much the same whether there is no form of government at all, or whether people agree that it shall be monarchical but lay down no way of knowing or designating the person who is to have the power and be the monarch. Whoever comes to exercise any part of the power by ways other than those the laws of the community have prescribed has no right to be obeyed, even though the form of the commonwealth is still preserved. He is not the person the laws have appointed, and so he is not the person the people have consented to. Nor can such a usurper, or anyone who derives his claim from him, ever have a title until the people are both free to consent and have actually consented to allow and confirm in him the power he has until then usurped.
